title: The Word clears doubt
hookLine: the Guru's Word cuts through doubt like light through dark (Anand)

lines: TWO IN THE MORNING, A DOUBT MOVES IN.
IT WAITS FOR THE NEXT QUIET.
cards: It's two in the morning and a doubt has moved in. Did I make the right choice? Do they actually like me?
Is any of this real? You try to argue it away. You list the reasons.
You check your phone for reassurance. None of it works, because doubt doesn't leave when it loses an argument. It just waits for the next quiet moment.
One pauri of Anand Sahib is about exactly this, and it says something surprising about what clears it.

teach.b: The word for doubt here is sahsaa, an anxious, uncertain, divided state of mind. The pauri starts by ruling things out.
In paraphrase: through rituals, sahaj, that settled ease, does not arise, and without sahaj, doubt does not go. However many disciplines you keep or deeds you perform, doubt doesn't leave.
The soul is stained by doubt; what discipline could wash it clean?

teach.h: WASH THE MIND WITH THE WORD.
teach.b: Then the answer: wash the mind by attaching it to the Word, the shabad, and keep your awareness on the Lord. Says Nanak, by the Guru's grace sahaj wells up, and this doubt departs.
So the chain runs: doubt goes when sahaj comes, and sahaj comes through the Word and the Guru's grace, not through rituals. The pauri's own picture is washing: doubt a stain, the Word clean water.

teach.h: LIKE A LIGHT, NOT AN ARGUMENT.
teach.b: Here's a second picture, not the pauri's own: a light in a dark room. Nobody argues with the dark or pushes it out piece by piece; the light goes on, and the dark is gone.
That's how the pauri treats the shabad: not as a better argument, but as something that changes the room.
It's one reason some Sikhs keep kirtan playing at home, or recite gurbani when the mind is unsettled: to let the Word fill the space the doubt was living in. One honest note.

The pauri isn't saying you'll never have a question. Sikhs ask hard questions; the Gurus asked them too. Sahsaa is the anxious, gnawing kind, the kind that stains, and that, the pauri says, the Word washes.

how: Many Sikhs recite this pauri as part of the full forty-pauri Anand Sahib in the morning Nitnem, and many keep kirtan or recited gurbani playing at home, especially at anxious times.

o: a ritual that washes away wrongdoing
anxious doubt that gnaws and stains the mind
an honest question asked of the Gurus

games.q: the Word clears doubt — tap the pairs.
p: the Word that washes the mind

s: the pauri says rituals clear doubt
it says doubt doesn't go however many disciplines you keep; the Word washes the mind.
in the pauri, doubt goes when sahaj, settled ease, wells up
by the Guru's grace sahaj wells up, and this doubt departs.
the pauri means a Sikh should never ask a hard question
sahsaa is the gnawing, anxious kind of doubt; the Gurus themselves asked hard questions.

games.q: it's two in the morning and a doubt is gnawing at you. according to this pauri, what clears it?
o: attaching the mind to the Word, until sahaj wells up.
games.why: man dhovahu sabad laagahu: wash the mind by attaching it to the Word. by the Guru's grace sahaj wells up, and the doubt departs.

practice: Write down one doubt that's been gnawing at you, in a single short sentence, on paper or your phone, without solving it or arguing with it; just put it where you can see it. Then turn it over, sit, and breathe slowly.
If you pray, you can let Waheguru fill the space where the doubt was, or play a shabad you love; if not, rest in the quiet after the writing.

wordCard.voice: Sahsaa, anxious doubt. It stains the mind, and isn't cleared by rituals; it goes when the Word washes the mind and sahaj wells up.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sahsaa, anxious, divided doubt; in Anand, it goes only when sahaj wells up.

carryVoice: Your line: the word clears. A doubt can lose its grip without ever losing an argument. Three hundred eighty-nine days now.

sources.ref: Anand Sahib, the pauri beginning 'karmee sahaj na upjai', Ang 918
